cards.heading: Why NAT exists
cards.body: Private RFC 1918 addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) aren't routed on the internet. At the network edge, NAT rewrites the private source address of outgoing packets to a public one and reverses it for the replies. Mark interfaces as 'ip nat inside' or 'ip nat outside'.
cards.example:
interface Gi0/0
 ip nat inside
interface Gi0/1
 ip nat outside

cards.heading: The four NAT addresses
cards.body: Inside/outside says whose device it is. Local/global says where you're looking from: local is the address as seen on the inside network, global is the address as seen on the outside.
cards.example:
Inside local    192.168.1.10   the PC's real address
Inside global   198.51.100.2   the PC after translation
Outside global  203.0.113.80   the server's real address
Outside local   203.0.113.80   the server as seen inside (usually the same)
cards.mnemonic:
Each name answers two questions. Inside or outside: whose host is it, ours or theirs? Local or global: who's looking, the inside network or the world?
Inside local is our PC as we see it (private). Inside global is our PC as the world sees it (public). Outside global is their server as the world sees it. Outside local is their server as we see it, usually the same address.

cards.heading: Static, dynamic and PAT
cards.body: Static NAT maps one inside address to one public address permanently (servers). Dynamic NAT hands out addresses from a pool. PAT (overload) lets many hosts share one address by also translating port numbers. PAT is what nearly every network uses. Static NAT is the one that lets internet hosts start connections to an inside server, because the mapping always exists; PAT and dynamic entries are only created by outbound traffic. Without 'overload', dynamic NAT needs a whole public address per inside host: when the pool is used up, new hosts aren't translated and fail until an entry times out.
cards.example:
ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.10 198.51.100.20
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUB
ip nat inside source list 1 interface Gi0/1 overload

cards.heading: Reading the translation table
cards.body: 'show ip nat translations' lists one row per translation. With PAT each row is an ip:port pair, and the inside global port keeps flows from different hosts apart. Many inside hosts sharing one inside global address, told apart by port, means PAT. If two hosts use the same source port, the router changes one of them (51000 became 1024 above).
